prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Palo Alto Networks Inc" (ticker PANW), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PANW", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Palo Alto Networks, Inc.
result.industry: Cybersecurity software and network security platforms
markets: Network security (next-generation firewalls, hardware and software)
Secure access service edge (SASE) and SD-WAN (Prisma Access, Prisma SD-WAN)
Security operations: SIEM, XDR, SOAR, attack-surface management (Cortex XSIAM, XDR, XSOAR, Xpanse)
Cloud security (Cortex Cloud, formerly Prisma Cloud)
Identity security: privileged access management, IAM, identity governance (Idira, from CyberArk)

mission.statement: to be the cybersecurity partner of choice, protecting our digital way of life
mission.source: Palo Alto Networks Form 10-K for fiscal year ended July 31, 2026
mission.plain: It wants to be the company everyone trusts to keep their computers, networks and data safe from hackers.

about.plain: Palo Alto Networks makes tools that keep hackers out of companies' computer systems. It started with smart 'firewalls', which are like security guards checking everything that goes in and out of a company's network. Today it also sells cloud software that watches for attacks, protects apps in the cloud, controls who can log in to what, and uses AI to spot and stop threats fast. Most customers pay a yearly subscription.
about.customers: Big companies, governments and other organisations that need to protect their computer networks, cloud apps and staff logins.
about.everyday: When you shop online, use your bank's app or log in at work, there is a good chance a Palo Alto Networks firewall or cloud service is checking that traffic for hackers.

money.plain: yearly cloud security services, security operations software and support contracts
controlling and protecting staff and machine logins and passwords
software that watches how cloud apps are running

money.part: AI security (Prisma AIRS, Portkey AI gateway, Koi agentic endpoint)
money.plain: protecting AI apps and AI agents from misuse and attacks

result.summary: Palo Alto Networks has a durable competitive advantage built on the largest share of the network security market (28.4% in 2024 per Omdia), deep integration into customers' networks, and a platform that now spans firewalls, SASE, security operations, cloud, identity and AI security. Its 'platformization' strategy raises switching costs, and Next-Generation Security ARR grew 63% to $9.10 billion in Q4 FY2026, helped by the CyberArk acquisition. The advantage is real but contested: Fortinet is cheaper in firewalls, CrowdStrike and Microsoft are strong in endpoint and security operations, and Zscaler leads in pure cloud SASE.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross margin stayed around 70-73% (70.4% in FY2026, 73.4% in FY2025) while revenue grew from $6,892.7M in FY2023 to $11,480M in FY2026, showing it sells at premium prices; but its platformization push since FY2024 has relied on free-of-charge transition periods and bundled discounts to win platform deals, and Fortinet competes hard on price in firewalls.

moats.evidence: Among enterprise security buyers Palo Alto Networks is a top-tier brand, a long-time Gartner Magic Quadrant leader in network firewalls, and its Unit 42 threat-intelligence team is widely cited.
Firewalls and security policies sit at the core of corporate networks and are costly and risky to rip out; RPO reached $21.2B (up 34%) at July 31, 2026, showing long multi-year commitments.

Threat data from its large installed base of firewalls, endpoints and cloud deployments feeds its detection models and services, so more customers make protection better for all, a data network effect rather than a classic two-sided one.

With $11.48B revenue in FY2026 and more than 8,700 channel partners, it can outspend most pure-play rivals on R&D and acquisitions (CyberArk ~$25B, Chronosphere), but it is not the low-cost producer: Fortinet's custom ASICs give it cheaper firewall hardware.
Cybersecurity is a large, fragmented market with many well-funded competitors, so no niche is naturally limited to one supplier.

Its integrated platform plus free-transition 'platformization' offers are hard for single-product vendors to match without hurting their own pricing, though Microsoft can bundle security even more cheaply.

It has a repeatable playbook of buying startups (Demisto, Twistlock, Bridgecrew, Talon, CyberArk, Chronosphere, Koi, Portkey) and integrating them into its sales machine, but rivals also acquire actively.
It owns no exclusive resource; its strengths are know-how, installed base and data rather than patents or licenses that competitors cannot get.

customers.evidence: RPO grew 34% to $21.2B and NGS ARR grew 63% to $9.10B at the end of FY2026, showing customers keep renewing and expanding; no single end-customer exceeded 10% of revenue in fiscal 2024-2026.

talent.evidence: Headcount rose from 16,068 to 21,921 in FY2026 (about 4,223 from CyberArk) and it pays well with heavy stock compensation, but it is not regularly at the top of major 'best places to work' rankings and acquired-company integration can cause staff turnover.

product.evidence: It is a long-standing Gartner Magic Quadrant Leader for network firewalls and SSE/SASE, and Cortex XSIAM is one of the leading AI-driven security-operations platforms; its breadth (network, cloud, SOC, identity, AI security) is matched by few rivals.

competitors.name: Fortinet
competitors.note: Firewalls, SD-WAN and SASE; the main price competitor in network security.

competitors.name: CrowdStrike
competitors.note: Endpoint/XDR, next-gen SIEM, cloud security and identity protection versus Cortex.

competitors.name: Zscaler
competitors.note: Cloud security service edge (SSE/SASE) versus Prisma Access.

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Defender, Sentinel SIEM, Entra identity and cloud security bundled with Microsoft licences.

competitors.name: Okta
competitors.note: Identity and access management versus Idira (CyberArk).

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Cloud Security, Wiz, Mandiant)
competitors.note: Cloud security, SIEM/SecOps and threat intelligence/incident response.

threats: Microsoft bundling Defender, Sentinel and Entra into enterprise licences at little extra cost
Fortinet's lower-cost ASIC-based firewalls and SASE winning price-sensitive deals
CrowdStrike and Zscaler expanding into its platform areas (SIEM, cloud, SASE)
Integration risk and dilution from the ~$25B CyberArk deal (diluted shares rose from 709M in FY2025 to 817M in Q4 FY2026) and other acquisitions; GAAP net income fell to $307M in FY2026 from $1,134M
Platformization free-transition offers pressuring near-term billings and margins
Security incidents or vulnerabilities in its own products (e.g., the 2024 PAN-OS CVE-2024-3400 zero-day) damaging trust
Heavy reliance on two distributors (30% of FY2026 revenue)

ceo.name: Nikesh Arora
ceo.background: Electrical engineering degree from IIT (BHU) Varanasi, MBA from Northeastern University and MS in finance from Boston College; former Google chief business officer and SoftBank president

c1.evidence: Palo Alto Networks leads network security with 28.4% share in 2024 (Omdia) and its NGS ARR grew 63% to $9.10B in Q4 FY2026, in a cybersecurity industry still growing fast with cloud and AI.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for best-in-class firewalls and the broadest integrated platform (network, SASE, Cortex SOC, cloud, identity via CyberArk, AI security), which is hard to copy, but Fortinet, CrowdStrike, Zscaler and Microsoft compete closely in each area.

c3.evidence: It is the default leader among enterprise security buyers, but ordinary consumers rarely know the name because it sells only to businesses and governments.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to be the cybersecurity partner of choice, protecting our digital way of life' is repeated in filings and matters for society, but management communication focuses heavily on ARR, platformization and financial targets.

c6.evidence: “firewall leader, cybersecurity giant, expensive, acquisitive”: among IT professionals and investors the impression is mostly positive, as a top-quality but premium-priced security vendor.

c7.evidence: Cybersecurity spending is a large, growing market riding secular trends in cloud, remote work and AI, and the company has expanded its addressable market with identity (CyberArk), observability (Chronosphere) and AI security (Prisma AIRS).

c8.evidence: It keeps entering big adjacent markets: identity security (CyberArk, closed February 2026), observability (Chronosphere, January 2026), AI agent and AI gateway security (Koi, Portkey, Console).

m1.evidence: Nikesh Arora set out the 'platformization' strategy in early 2024 and has pushed the company early into AI security and AI-driven security operations (XSIAM), a clear view of where security is going.

m2.evidence: Arora is not the founder (Nir Zuk founded the company in 2005) but has led it since 2018 with bold, long-term bets such as the ~$25B CyberArk purchase, though his very large stock-based pay packages drew criticism.

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way of a servant-leadership style; Arora is known as a demanding, sales-driven leader.

m5.evidence: Under Arora the company built a culture of fast acquisition and integration (Bridgecrew, Talon, Dig, CyberArk, Chronosphere) and new products like XSIAM and Prisma AIRS, though much innovation is bought rather than home-grown.

m6.evidence: Arora has an electrical engineering degree but his career has been in business, sales and finance (Google, SoftBank); CTO and founder Nir Zuk has led product technology.

m7.evidence: No standout public record of causes beyond the business; his stewardship mainly emphasises protecting customers' digital lives.

m7b.evidence: No verified record found of Nikesh Arora giving a commencement speech at a top university such as Stanford, Harvard or MIT.

m8b.evidence: Arora is a well-known, outspoken and highly paid tech executive, but not a cultural personality on the level of Elon Musk or Alex Karp.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2018 revenue grew from $3,408.4M in FY2020 to $11,480M in FY2026, and the company shifted to mostly subscription revenue (80% in FY2026).

m10.evidence: Palo Alto Networks is not known for frugality; it pays rich stock compensation and has spent heavily on acquisitions (e.g., about $25B for CyberArk).

c10.evidence: Its products protect banks, hospitals, governments and businesses used by billions of people worldwide, but the benefit is indirect, preventing harm rather than being something people use directly.

p2.evidence: Stopping well-funded criminal and nation-state hackers across networks, cloud, identities and AI agents is technically very hard and vital to the digital economy.

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin improved from -7.1% in FY2021 to 13.5% in FY2025 before falling to 6.1% in FY2026 on CyberArk acquisition costs, while gross margin was about flat (70.0% in FY2021, 70.4% in FY2026).

f3.evidence: At July 31, 2026 it had $1,774M of convertible notes versus $7,906M of cash and investments and $4,553M of FY2026 operating cash flow, with stockholders' equity of $27,492M.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from -$304.1M in FY2021 to $1,242.9M in FY2025 but fell to $695M in FY2026, while operating cash flow rose to $4,553M in FY2026 from $3,716M in FY2025.

v1.evidence: Its firewalls are widely seen as the gold standard, and the practical reason to choose it is one integrated platform covering network, cloud, SOC and identity, but rivals beat it on price (Fortinet) or in single areas (CrowdStrike endpoint, Zscaler SSE).

v2.evidence: It has a good reputation as a well-paying tech employer but no verified top placement in major rankings such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: If it disappeared, tens of thousands of enterprises and government agencies would lose the firewalls and security services guarding their networks, leaving banks, hospitals and infrastructure more exposed to cyberattacks.
